milestone.title: Amiga Lorraine's first press demonstration
milestone.note: The secret Winter CES prototype previewed the custom-chip multimedia architecture that would define the Amiga and influence graphics, sound and gaming computers for years.

editorNote: Extra Edition: Winter CES opens a decisive year with new Commodore machines and a private glimpse of Amiga’s next-generation Lorraine prototype.
morningLine: LAS VEGAS — A crowded Commodore stand and a secret Amiga demonstration set the pace as the home-computer business enters its shakeout year.

lead.headline: Commodore's 264 family steals a shakeout-era Winter CES
lead.dek: Commodore draws the Winter CES crowds with two 64K machines, built-in productivity software and a new BASIC—while leaving price and compatibility questions open.
body: The International Winter Consumer Electronics Show opened in Las Vegas on January 7 and ran through January 10; COMPUTE! estimated attendance at 80,000-90,000 and said the Commodore stand was crowded throughout the show. Commodore announced the 264 and speech-equipped 364V, both with 64K RAM and a 7501-family processor running at about 1.76 MHz.

The machines used the TED chip, offered 16 colors at eight luminance levels (128 shades), but omitted the Commodore 64's sprites and sophisticated SID-style three-voice sound, providing two simpler tone generators instead. BASIC 3.5 added structured-programming, graphics, sound, disk, error-trapping and editing commands; more than 59K was available to BASIC versus about 38K on the Commodore 64.

Buyers were to choose built-in ROM software such as Superscript, EasyCalc, 3-Plus-1, Logo, PILOT or Magic Desk II; the 364V added a numeric keypad and speech synthesis. No firm price was announced. Commodore told COMPUTE! the 264 would retail below $500 and the 364V slightly higher; Creative Computing reported industry guesses near $300 and below $500 respectively.

Compatibility was mixed: 1541 serial drives and some user-port devices would work, but old Datasette units, joysticks and Commodore 64 cartridges would not because connectors and the cartridge port changed. COMPUTE! described this CES as the start of the long-predicted home-computer shakeout: Atari had canceled the 1400XL, IBM stayed away after showing PCjr at COMDEX, and Texas Instruments displayed no TI-99/4A after quitting the market.

stories.headline: Behind a secret CES door, Amiga shows 'Lorraine'
body: Creative Computing editor John J. Anderson saw Lorraine privately at Winter CES; it was absent from Amiga's public booth and still built from breadboards, with production custom chips expected in April or May. Amiga president Dave Morse said sales of the company's Joyboard and other accessories had helped bankroll the computer project.

The custom VLSI chipset was designed by Jay Miner, designer of the original Atari computer chipset. The prototype delivered multicolor real-time animation, sprites, NTSC and RGB output, and four-voice stereo sound intended to feed a home sound system.

The planned machine had 128K RAM, a high-density 5.25-inch disk drive and a ROM cartridge slot; Anderson inferred a 68000-class processor but Morse did not confirm it. Amiga said it would cost less than a fully configured IBM PCjr; IBM compatibility was contemplated through an add-on processor cartridge.

stories.headline: Home-computer boom gives way to a fight for survival
body: COMPUTE! found far fewer new home computers than at the previous summer show, when 17 new machines had appeared. Atari showed its XL line but had officially canceled the 1400XL and offered only vague statements on the 1450XLD.

Spectravideo dropped the SV-318 in favor of an upgraded SV-328 Mark II and the SVI-728 MSX. Spectravideo's booth demonstration mocked Coleco's Adam by sawing one in half and dropping it into a trash can while a flushing sound played; Coleco representative Barbara Wruck said show management had forced removal of a real toilet used on the first day.
Apple attended but held Macintosh for its stockholders meeting later in January; IBM did not attend, having shown PCjr at COMDEX.

stories.headline: Kodak jumps into home video with a one-piece 8mm camcorder
body: Eastman Kodak unveiled its one-piece 8mm color camera-recorder system in New York on January 4, entering the home-video market. Contemporary reports emphasized that the unit combined camera and recorder rather than requiring a separate deck.

RCA simultaneously unveiled a 2.2-pound palm-sized color video camera but predicted 8mm consumer adoption would wait until 1985 or 1986. The Kodak announcement came immediately before Winter CES and represented a direct challenge to established VHS and Betamax equipment.

computerItems.title: Commodore 264
computerItems.summary: 64K, 7501-family CPU at roughly 1.76 MHz, TED graphics/sound, BASIC 3.5, built-in application ROM option, over 59K BASIC workspace; announced below $500 with April 1 target.

computerItems.title: Commodore 364V
computerItems.summary: 264 derivative with 19-key numeric keypad, Magic Voice speech synthesizer and extra ROM capacity; price expected somewhat above the 264 but under $500 in Creative Computing's estimate.

computerItems.title: Amiga Lorraine prototype
computerItems.summary: Private breadboard demo with Jay Miner custom chips, 128K planned RAM, four-voice stereo, sprite animation, RGB/NTSC output and high-density 5.25-inch drive.

softwareList.name: Commodore 3-Plus-1
softwareList.detail: Prototype integrated package for the 264 combining word processing, file management, spreadsheet and business graphics, shown as a built-in ROM option.

softwareList.name: Magic Desk II and BASIC 3.5
softwareList.detail: Magic Desk II offered a Lisa-like icon interface with editor, spreadsheet, file manager and calculator; BASIC 3.5 supplied long-missing graphics, sound, disk and structured-programming commands.

briefs.headline: Apple saves Macintosh for later in January
briefs.text: Apple returned to CES after roughly three years but did not show Macintosh, reserving its unveiling for the company's stockholders meeting later in the month.

briefs.headline: Atari officially drops the 1400XL
briefs.text: Atari's CES display featured its existing XL range minus the canceled 1400XL; the future of the 1450XLD remained vague.

periodAd.headline: 64K Computing—Built In
periodAd.summary: Commodore’s 264 family promises BASIC 3.5 and a choice of productivity software in ROM.
periodAd.tagline: The next home office may start below $500.

market.headline: The shakeout reaches the show floor
market.summary: Fewer new home computers, canceled models and missing former competitors make Winter CES a test of survival as much as innovation.

worldAnchor.headline: Syria frees captured U.S. Navy flier after Jesse Jackson mission
worldAnchor.summary: On January 3 Syria agreed to release Lt. Robert O. Goodman Jr., shot down and captured during a December raid over Lebanon. President Reagan publicly welcomed the decision and credited Jackson's efforts; Goodman flew out with Jackson early January 4.

gadgetWatch.headline: Kodak unveils one-piece 8mm color camcorder
gadgetWatch.summary: Kodak entered home video on January 4 with a compact integrated camera-recorder built around the emerging 8mm format, challenging the bulkier camera-plus-deck model and established VHS/Beta ecosystem.
